newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Prospect of drug-related terror returns to Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Prospect of drug-related terror returns to Colombia.

text.p: The specter of drug-related terror returned to Colombia on Tuesday after police defused a powerful car bomb they said was planted by drug lords in the heart of the country's second largest city.

"This definitely has to be the work of drug traffickers," National Police chief Gen. Rosso Jose Serrano said of the bomb, 360 pounds (163 kg) of dynamite and a smaller amount of C-4 explosive. The deadly device was discovered at 3:28 a.m. (8:28 GMT) in the centre of the southwestern city of Cali.

"This should serve as a warning to all Colombians," Serrano added, saying drug traffickers opposed to extradition were apparently planning to unleash a wave of "narco-violence and narco-terrorism" like the one that swept Colombia in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

Extradition was banned by Congress in 1991 in a bid to end a campaign of bombings, assassinations and kidnappings that drug traffickers led by Pablo Escobar, the late and notoriously violent leader of the Medellin drug cartel, waged in the name of a group known as "The Extraditables."

A Senate panel approved a bill to lift the ban last month and Justice Minister Carlos Medellin told reporters last week that drug kingpins already serving time in Colombian jails may soon face the prospect of being tried in foreign courts.

Police said pamphlets signed by a previously unknown group calling itself the "Movement for National Sovereignty" were found near the car bomb and elsewhere in Cali on Tuesday, where graffiti opposing extradition has appeared across the city since last month.
The pamphlets, reminiscent of those Escobar circulated, attack extradition as a violation of Colombian sovereignty and threaten reprisals against lawmakers who approve it.

"Things have been heating up here for a while now," a judicial official in Cali said in a telephone interview when asked about the pamphlets and car bomb placed in San Nicolas, a densely populated city centre district.
"There's a lot of fear," he added, saying memories of the "narco-bombs" that claimed hundreds of lives in Bogota and Medellin in the 1980s were still fresh in Colombians' minds.
Serrano, speaking on Caracol radio, said an anonymous telephone caller tipped police off about the bomb.

A police spokeswoman in Cali said the bomb was in a mini-bus reported stolen 15 days ago, which was parked outside a chemical plant belonging to a family member of Sen. Claudia Blum, a sponsor of the bill lifting the extradition ban.
The spokeswoman said it was not clear if there was a link between the device and two small bombs detonated on Monday night outside a Cali police academy. They caused minor damage but no injuries.
